newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan mills see glitches in raw sugar import.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan mills see glitches in raw sugar import.

text.p: Pakistani sugar mills on Thursday welcomed the government's decision to allow duty-free import of raw sugar for re-export after refining but said the policy needed to be further smoothed out.

"It is a good move and worth trying but the condition of exporting the same quantity that has been refined after importing raws will cause problems," Pakistan Sugar Mills Association secretarty-general Ali Qazilbash told Reuters.
Commerce Minister Ishaq Dar announced in the trade policy for fiscal 1997/98 (July-June) on Wednesday permission for duty-free import of raw sugar for export after refining.
He told a news conference on Thursday that the government expected to import a million tonnes of raw sugar in 1997/98 for export after refining.
Qazilbash said the time for importing raw sugar and its export after refining would have to be settled if the imported raw could not be sold in the domestic market.
"If we have to keep the imported raw separate from local cane, then raw imports will only be possible after the end of the domestic crushing season," he said.

"This will create problems as almost all the mills use biogas generated from burning crushed cane as fuel for running their boilers. If the imported raw is refined after the end of the crushing season, they will have to use furnace oil, which will cost much more than biogas."
He said the policy in its present form would be more beneficial to sugar mills close to port city of Karachi compared to those in the north that would bear additional transport costs.

Imports of cheaper raw sugar instead of refined white crystal sugar could save at least $50 million a year in foreign exchange and allow mills, now operating seasonally at 50 percent of their capacity, to run full capacity throughout the year, he said.
Pakistan, hit by low cane production, imported 596,467 tonnes of refined sugar worth $227 million in June-July 1996/97, compared to a negligible 3,480 tonnes in the year-ago period.
